steps.body: Two-way tables reveal **association** between categories. Compare relative frequencies across rows: if children and adults prefer dogs at very different rates, age and pet-preference are **associated**. Similar rates mean little or no association.
Build a survey design that can compare age groups without selection bias.

widget.prompt: Study age and pet preference across a town. Choose a design that represents both age groups, use at least 120 people, and repeat it.
widget.successFeedback: A stratified sample represents both age groups; repeated larger samples stabilize the relative-frequency comparison.
widget.methodFeedback: Sampling only one convenient location can confound age with where people were recruited.
widget.sizeFeedback: Keep the stratified design and increase the sample to stabilize subgroup rates.
widget.drawsFeedback: Repeat the design so the association is not based on one unusually lucky sample.

cml.actionGoal: Design a fair categorical association study before comparing rates.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Make the sample ten times larger without changing a biased method. Which problem remains?

explanation.prompt: Why can a very large convenience sample still be misleading?

options.label: It can repeatedly overrepresent the same easy-to-reach group.
options.feedback: Exactly — size cannot repair a biased selection process.

options.label: Large samples are always accurate.
options.feedback: Large samples can be precisely wrong when selection is biased.

options.label: Repeat the same biased selection many times.

predict.reveal: A larger sample reduces random variability, but only representative selection addresses systematic bias.

steps.body: The key move is comparing **rates, not raw counts**. Two groups of different sizes can't be compared by counts alone. Turning each into a percent of its own row makes a fair comparison possible.

explanationVariants: Groups of different sizes must be compared by rates, since raw counts can mislead.
Rates make unequal-sized groups comparable; counts alone don't.

widget.prompt: Why compare relative frequencies (rates) instead of raw counts across rows?

options.label: The rows can have different totals, so counts alone aren't a fair comparison
options.feedback: Right — rates adjust for different group sizes, making a fair comparison.

options.label: Counts are always wrong
options.feedback: Counts aren't wrong — they're just unfair to compare when groups differ in size, so use rates.

options.label: Rates are easier to add
options.feedback: The reason is fairness across different-sized groups, not ease of adding.

options.label: Percents are always bigger
options.feedback: Percents aren't bigger — they make different-sized groups comparable.

widget.prompt: In a table, 70% of teens and 68% of adults chose the same brand. Are choice and age strongly associated?

options.label: No — the rates are nearly equal, so little association
options.feedback: Right — similar rates across groups mean little or no association.

options.label: Yes — strongly associated
options.feedback: Strong association needs DIFFERENT rates — 70% vs 68% are nearly equal, so little association.

options.label: Yes — because both are high
options.feedback: High rates alone don't show association — it's the DIFFERENCE that matters, and these barely differ.

options.label: Can't tell from rates
options.feedback: You CAN tell: nearly-equal rates (70% vs 68%) mean little association.

explanationVariants: 90% vs 30% is a large gap, so the two categories are strongly associated.
A big rate difference (90% vs 30%) signals a strong association.

widget.prompt: Among students, 90% of athletes but only 30% of non-athletes ate breakfast. Are being an athlete and eating breakfast associated?

options.label: Yes — the rates differ a lot (90% vs 30%)
options.feedback: Right — a large difference in rates signals a strong association.

options.label: No association
options.feedback: 90% vs 30% is a HUGE gap — that's a strong association, not none.

options.label: Only if the groups are equal size
options.feedback: Rates already adjust for size — the 90% vs 30% gap shows association regardless.

options.label: Can't tell
options.feedback: The big rate gap (90% vs 30%) clearly shows an association.

explanationVariants: Of 20 adults, 15 prefer cats: 15 ÷ 20 = 75%, versus 10 ÷ 30 ≈ 33% of children — a big gap.
Adults: 75% cats; children: 33% cats — very different, so associated.

widget.prompt: Use the adult row as the comparison group. What percent of adults prefer cats?

answerChoices.feedback: Yes. The highlighted cell is 15 and the adult-row total is 20, so 15 ÷ 20 = 75%.
30% uses all 50 people as the denominator. The question says 'of adults,' so use the adult-row total, 20.

answerChoices.label: 15 people
answerChoices.feedback: 15 is the cell count. A relative frequency compares that count with the 20 adults: 15 ÷ 20 = 75%.

widget.successFeedback: The table shows 15 of 20 adults in the cat column: 15 ÷ 20 = 75%. The children are at 10 of 30, about 33%, so the row rates differ sharply.
widget.explorationFeedback: Switch to the row named by 'of adults' before choosing a rate.
widget.conditionFeedback: Use the adult row as the denominator; a column or the whole table answers a different question.
widget.cellFeedback: Use the adult-and-cat intersection as the numerator.

explanationVariants: Children like cats at 10 ÷ 30 ≈ 33%; adults at 15 ÷ 20 = 75%. The rates differ sharply, so age and preference are associated.
33% vs 75% is a big gap — associated.

widget.prompt: Children prefer cats at about 33% (10 of 30); adults at 75% (15 of 20). What do these rates show?

options.label: Age and pet preference are associated — the rates differ sharply
options.feedback: Right — 33% vs 75% is a large gap, showing a clear association.

options.label: No association — cats appear in both rows
options.feedback: Appearing in both rows isn't the test — the RATES (33% vs 75%) differ sharply, so associated.

options.label: Nothing, since counts differ
options.feedback: The rates already adjust for the different totals — 33% vs 75% shows association.

options.label: Adults and children are the same
options.feedback: They're clearly different: 33% vs 75% cat-preference — an association.

hints: Compare the two cat-preference rates: 33% (children) vs 75% (adults).
A large gap between the rates means the categories are associated.
33% vs 75% is a big gap, so age and preference ARE associated.

steps.body: Compare relative frequencies across rows: differing rates show association; similar rates don't. That completes Grade 8.
takeaways: Compare rates (relative frequencies), not raw counts, across groups.
Sharply different rates signal association between the categories.
Nearly equal rates mean little or no association.
steps.teaser: That completes Bivariate Statistics — and all of Grade 8 math.

concept.body: To spot association in a two-way table, compare relative frequencies (rates) across rows. Sharply different rates signal association; similar rates mean little or none. Compare rates, not raw counts, because groups can differ in size.

explanationVariants: 80% vs 78% are nearly equal, so there's little association.
Similar rates (80% vs 78%) mean little association.
